title: 15 New Jersey museums and historic sites worth the drive
dek: From Edison's lab in West Orange to a battleship on the Delaware, here is what to see at each stop, how easy it is to get around, and what seniors pay.
keyFacts: Princeton University Art Museum, the Zimmerli at Rutgers and the New Jersey State Museum charge no general admission.
Morristown National Historical Park collects no entrance fee.
Thomas Edison National Historical Park charges $15 per person 16 and older. The federal Senior Pass (62+) is accepted.
Grounds For Sculpture requires an advance timed ticket. Seniors 65+ pay $18.
Many museums lend wheelchairs free, first come, first served. Call ahead to hold one.
body:
New Jersey packs a lot of history and art into a small state. You can stand in Thomas Edison's laboratory in the morning and be eating lunch in Princeton an hour later. Most of the places below are easy on the knees, and several are free.

We checked every price and access detail on each museum's own website in October 2026. Where a museum does not post a senior rate, we say so. Hours change often, especially as the season turns, so call before you set out.

The best museum day is the one where you know where the elevator and the bench are before you arrive.

North Jersey: which museums are closest to home?

1. The Newark Museum of Art, Newark

This big downtown museum sits at 49 Washington Street. Highlights include the Victorian Ballantine House and a planetarium with its own $10 ticket. It is open Thursday through Sunday, noon to 5 p.m.

Getting around: The museum calls its campus fully accessible, with elevators to all galleries and levels. Free manual wheelchairs and portable stools are lent at the Welcome Center. The Bamberger entrance on Washington Street has a ramp and an automatic door.

Parking: There is no on-site parking during construction. The museum points visitors to nearby garages, including the Hahne & Co. garage on New Street. Street meters are free on Sundays.

Senior price: $8 for visitors 65 and older (adults pay $10). Newark residents get in free.

2. Montclair Art Museum, Montclair

A comfortable, manageable museum known for its American and Native American art. Galleries are open to the public Friday and Saturday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. A free guided tour runs Sundays at 2 p.m.

Getting around: All public areas are wheelchair accessible. Both entrances have push-button doors, and cars can pull up to the front to drop off passengers. The on-site lot is free, with accessible spaces near the entrances.

Senior price: $12 for seniors (adults pay $17). Library cardholders should ask whether their library has a museum membership card, which admits two adults. Questions: 973-746-5555.

3. Paterson Great Falls National Historical Park, Paterson

The Passaic River drops about 77 feet here between dark basalt cliffs. This is where Alexander Hamilton pictured an industrial city, and the mill buildings still stand around it. The view from the overlook railing is free.

Getting around: Overlook Park has accessible parking spaces. Paths mix paved and unpaved sections, and some city sidewalks are narrow or steep. The park lends no wheelchairs. There is no visitor center right now and no restrooms in the park. Accessible restrooms are at the Paterson Museum, 2 Market Street. Park office: 973-523-0370.

4. Thomas Edison National Historical Park, West Orange

Walk through the laboratory complex where Edison's team worked on the phonograph and motion pictures. Then drive up to Glenmont, his home in Llewellyn Park.

Getting around: Building 5, the main lab, has an elevator to the second and third floors. Benches line the tour route and sit outside several buildings. Manual wheelchairs are lent free. The Glenmont mansion is not wheelchair accessible and the tour has many steps, though you can see the house from accessible outdoor areas. Visitor center: 973-736-0550 ext. 11. See the park's accessibility page.

Price: $15 per person 16 and older, cards only. The America the Beautiful Senior Pass covers entry. It costs $20 a year or $80 for life if you are 62 or older.

5. Morris Museum, Morristown

Go for the Guinness Collection of mechanical musical instruments and automata, music boxes and moving figures that still play. Call ahead to ask when a demonstration is scheduled. Open Wednesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Getting around: Every public space is reached by elevator or ramp. A small supply of wheelchairs is kept at the admissions desk.

Senior price: $8 (general admission $12). Phone: 973-971-3700.

6. Morristown National Historical Park, Morristown

George Washington's army spent two hard winters here. See the Ford Mansion, which served as his headquarters, and the museum next door. Then drive the park roads at Jockey Hollow, where the soldiers camped.

Getting around: The headquarters museum and the Jockey Hollow Visitor Center are wheelchair accessible, with paved walks from the lots. More than 3 miles of paved roads at Jockey Hollow can be toured by car, which is a gentle option. Ask at the museum desk for the Ford Mansion accessibility book.

Price: No entrance fee. Buildings are generally open Thursday through Monday, 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Museum desk: 973-539-2016 ext. 210.

7. Liberty Hall Museum, Union

This mansion on the Kean University campus was home to William Livingston, New Jersey's first elected governor, and later generations of the Kean family. Tours run April 1 through the last Sunday in December, Wednesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Getting around: Be honest with yourself here. Walkways are gravel, and the museum says the mansion is not yet ADA compliant. A state grant is funding work to change that.

Senior price: $10 (adults $14). Phone: 908-527-0400.

Central Jersey: where can you see the most for the least?

8. Princeton University Art Museum, Princeton

The museum opened a new building on October 31, 2025, designed by Adjaye Associates. It spreads across three stories and nine connected pavilions. Admission is free to all. It stays open until 8 p.m. on Thursdays and Fridays.

Getting around: All three levels are reached by elevator. Wheelchairs and canes are lent at the information desk, and portable gallery stools are available. Driving onto campus for accessible drop-off or parking needs approval at least three business days ahead. Call 609-258-3788, option 1.

9. Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers, New Brunswick

The Zimmerli holds one of the largest collections of Soviet nonconformist art anywhere, and its Soviet and Eurasian holdings top 22,000 objects. It is also strong in French nineteenth-century prints and Japanese woodcuts. Admission is free.

Hours: Wednesday and Friday 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., Thursday 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., weekends noon to 5 p.m. Note that the Upper Dodge wing is temporarily closed.

Getting around: The museum asks for accommodation requests at least two weeks before your visit. Email the access coordinator at nls104@zimmerli.rutgers.edu.

10. Grounds For Sculpture, Hamilton

Landscaped gardens filled with large outdoor sculpture, plus indoor galleries. It is a walking museum, so plan your route.

Getting around: The main path is paved with paver stone. Side paths can be gravel or sand, narrow or steep. Wheelchairs rent for $15 a day and scooters for $29 for the first four hours, first come, first served. Bring a driver's license. Accessible parking is in the main lots.

Senior price: $18 for 65 and older (adults $25). Timed tickets must be booked online in advance. Closed Tuesdays from September through May.

11. New Jersey State Museum, Trenton

Natural history, archaeology, fine art and state history, all next to the State House. General admission is free. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

Getting around: Use the Planetarium entrance if walking is hard. Placard holders can park right in front. Every level has two elevators, most galleries have benches, and the front desk lends one free wheelchair and folding stools. Details are on the museum's accessibility page.

Senior price: Free for the museum. Planetarium shows are $10, with $1 off for seniors 65 and older.

12. Old Barracks Museum, Trenton

Built during the French and Indian War, the barracks housed Hessian soldiers before the Battle of Trenton in 1776. Costumed interpreters bring it to life. Open year-round, Wednesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Senior price: $12 (adults $15). Limited parking is in Lot 5A, across from the War Memorial. The museum's site does not describe accessibility, so call 609-396-1776 first.

South Jersey: what is worth a longer drive?

13. Battleship New Jersey, Camden

The Iowa-class battleship is docked on the Camden waterfront, across from Philadelphia. Fall hours are Thursday through Monday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., last ticket at 4 p.m.

Getting around: The ship is full of steep ladders. Wheelchair users can reach the main deck exterior, the anti-aircraft guns and the officers' wardroom, using elevators under the forward and aft entry stairs. There is a roughly 45-minute main deck tour that skips the ladders. To arrange accessible parking, call 1-866-877-6262 ext. 108. Lot parking runs $11 to $20.

Senior price: Not posted. Ask about senior rates when you buy tickets.

14. WheatonArts, Millville

Home of the Museum of American Glass and working studios where you can watch glassblowers and potters most days. Open April through December, Thursday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., rain or shine.

Senior price: $13 for 62 and older (adults $14). Give two weeks' notice for special accommodations.

15. Cape May MAC sites, Cape May

Cape May MAC runs the Emlen Physick Estate (an 1879 Victorian house), the Cape May Lighthouse, the World War II Lookout Tower and the town's trolley tours.

Getting around: The Physick Estate's first floor is reached through the south entrance, and a video covers the upstairs. The lighthouse has 199 steps and no elevator, but the Oil House exhibit at its base has a ramped entrance. The World War II Lookout Tower has 99 steps, with an accessible wooden walkway and ground floor. One trolley has a wheelchair lift. Reserve it at least two weeks ahead at 609-884-5404. Full details are on the Cape May MAC accessibility page.

Senior price: Not posted. Ask about senior rates.

How do I plan a museum day that does not wear me out?

  1. Call the day before. Confirm hours, ask if a wheelchair or stool can be set aside, and ask which entrance is easiest.
  2. Go early on a weekday. Crowds are thinner and staff have more time to help.
  3. Pick one wing. Two hours of looking is plenty. Sit down every 30 minutes, even if you feel fine.
  4. Bring your ID and any passes. That means your federal Senior Pass for national parks, and a library museum pass if your town offers one.
  5. Plan lunch near the museum. Princeton's museum has a restaurant, and Battleship New Jersey has a café.
Ask your library

Many New Jersey public libraries lend free or discounted museum passes. Ask at the circulation desk before you pay full price.

For more low-cost outings, see our guide to free and discounted things for NJ seniors and our list of easy day trips. If you would like to take a class at one of these museums, read learning something new after 60.

faq.q: Which New Jersey museums are free?
faq.a: Princeton University Art Museum, the Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers and the New Jersey State Museum charge no general admission. Morristown National Historical Park has no entrance fee. The Paterson Great Falls overlook is also free.

faq.q: Does the national park Senior Pass work at Thomas Edison's lab?
faq.a: Yes. Thomas Edison National Historical Park accepts America the Beautiful passes. The Senior Pass is $20 a year or $80 for life for U.S. citizens and residents 62 and older. Bring photo ID.

faq.q: Can I borrow a wheelchair at these museums?
faq.a: Many lend them free, including the Newark Museum of Art, Princeton University Art Museum, the Morris Museum, the New Jersey State Museum and the Edison park. Grounds For Sculpture rents them. Supplies are small, so call ahead.

faq.q: Which sites are hard for people who use a wheelchair?
faq.a: The Glenmont mansion at the Edison park, Liberty Hall in Union, the Cape May Lighthouse tower and most of Battleship New Jersey below the main deck. Each still has accessible areas or alternatives.

faq.q: Which New Jersey museums offer senior discounts?
faq.a: Many do. In October 2026 seniors paid $8 at the Newark Museum of Art and the Morris Museum, $10 at Liberty Hall, $12 at the Montclair Art Museum and the Old Barracks, $13 at WheatonArts and $18 at Grounds For Sculpture. Ages vary from 62 to 65, so bring ID.

faq.q: Do I need to book Grounds For Sculpture ahead of time?
faq.a: Yes. Grounds For Sculpture uses timed tickets, and if an entry time sells out online it is also sold out at the gate. It is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and closed Tuesdays from September through May.

title: New Jersey gardens and easy walks, with the benches and restrooms noted
dek: Arboretums, iris beds, cherry trees and flat paths along the canal and the bay. Here is what the ground is like at each one, where to sit, and when to go.
keyFacts: Duke Farms in Hillsborough has more than 15 miles of flat, paved trails. Trails are open Tuesday through Saturday.
Presby Iris Gardens in Upper Montclair usually blooms mid-May through the first week of June.
Branch Brook Park has more than 5,300 cherry trees. Peak bloom usually comes in April.
Skylands, the New Jersey State Botanical Garden, is always free to enter.
NJ residents 62+ can get a free State Parks Senior Citizen Pass. Call 1-800-843-6420.
body:
A good walk does not have to be a hike. New Jersey has gardens with paved paths, a canal towpath that stays level for miles, and a hawk platform where you can sit and watch the sky. This list is built around one question: can I enjoy this without worrying about my footing or finding a bathroom?

We checked each place's own website in October 2026 for path surfaces, restrooms and hours. Where a site does not say, we tell you to ask.

Ask three things before any walk. What is the ground like, where can I sit, and where is the restroom?

Which gardens have the smoothest paths?

Duke Farms, Hillsborough

Doris Duke's former estate covers 2,700 acres in Somerset County. It is the best choice on this list if you want distance without effort. Most of its more than 15 miles of trail are flat, paved and wider than 36 inches. Meadow and woodland trails are unpaved and marked with dotted lines on the property map.

  • Help getting around: A free accessibility transport runs between the Farm Barn Orientation Center and the Orchid Range for visitors with limited mobility. Reserve it ahead.
  • Restrooms: Accessible restrooms are in the Farm Barn and the Orchid Range. Composting toilets on the trails vary, and some have steps.
  • Benches: Several line the path to the Farm Barn entrance. One has both a backrest and armrests.
  • Hours: Trails are open Tuesday through Saturday from 8:30 a.m., with earlier closing in winter. Closed Sunday and Monday. Saturday visits in the busy season need a free parking pass, released on Monday afternoons.

Check the Duke Farms visit page for closures before you drive.

Best season: Spring and fall for walking. The Orchid Range is a warm stop in winter, though paths are not salted after storms.

Frelinghuysen Arboretum, Morris Township

This Morris County park has 28 garden areas and more than 3,200 kinds of plants around an 1891 mansion. The county describes many paved trails for easy strolls. Look for the Rose Garden and the dawn redwoods in the Pinetum.

  • Hours: Daily, 8 a.m. to sunset, all year. The county lists no admission fee.
  • Restrooms: Listed as an amenity. Ask at the Haggerty Center where the nearest one is.
  • Phone: 973-326-7601.

Best season: June for roses. Fall color is lovely too.

Reeves-Reed Arboretum, Summit

A small, gracious estate garden that is free to explore, with a suggested $10 donation. Grounds are open every day: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. from April through October, and 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. from November through March.

  • Surfaces: Much of the historic garden has ramps and paved paths. Some areas are hard to reach without help because the terrain varies. The arboretum is building a continuous accessible loop through its "A Path for All" project.
  • Accessible areas: The Visitors Center, Welcome Walk, Perennial Border, Wisner House gallery and patio.
  • Restrooms: Accessible ones are in Wisner House and the Stackhouse Education Center.
  • Parking: Accessible parking is limited, and no wheelchairs are available on site.

Grounds For Sculpture, Hamilton

Part garden, part outdoor museum. The main path is paved with paver stone and accessible, and accessible routes are marked on the online map. Smaller side paths are gravel or sand and can be narrow or steep. Wheelchairs rent for $15 a day and scooters for $29 for the first four hours, first come, first served. Seniors 65 and older pay $18, and timed tickets must be booked online. Closed Tuesdays from September through May. See the accessibility page before you go.

Best season: Fall, when the trees turn and the summer crowds are gone.

When should I go for flowers?

GardenPeak showCost
Branch Brook Park cherry blossoms, Newark and BellevilleUsually AprilFree
Skylands lilacs and crabapples, RingwoodMid to late springFree garden; summer weekend parking fee
Presby Iris Gardens, Upper MontclairMid-May to first week of JuneFree; $10 suggested donation

Branch Brook Park, Newark and Belleville

Essex County's Branch Brook Park has more than 5,300 Japanese flowering cherry trees in 18 varieties. Bloom usually peaks in the second and third weeks of April, though it came early in 2026, from about April 3 to 12. The thickest groves are near the Cherry Blossom Welcome Center, by the baseball diamonds. Because the collection is so varied, at least one variety is usually in bloom from late March to early May.

Easy on the legs: The county says you can drive from one end of the park to the other and see trees in bloom without leaving the car. That makes it one of the best flower trips in the state for someone with limited mobility. Benches throughout the park are first come, first served.

Tips: The park and parking are free. Park along the park roads behind the white lines, or in the Welcome Center lot, which has about 130 spaces. On festival race mornings the park closes to cars, so check the event schedule. The park is open sunrise to 10 p.m. Its website does not list restrooms, so plan a stop before you come.

Presby Memorial Iris Gardens, Upper Montclair

More than 10,000 irises of about 1,500 varieties, in a long strip along Upper Mountain Avenue. Bloom season usually runs mid-May through the first week of June, and some reblooming beds flower again in October. Admission is free, with a suggested $10 donation. Portable toilets are set up during bloom season.

Be ready for: Grass and uneven ground, with steep slopes in some beds. The garden itself says it is not fully accessible. A flat stone area beside the beds lets you view the flowers without crossing the grass. The Walther House and gift shop are up seven steps with a wooden handrail. There is no on-site parking, and street parking is limited at peak. Go on a weekday morning. Questions: presbyiris@verizon.net.

Skylands, the New Jersey State Botanical Garden, Ringwood

Formal gardens around a Tudor-style manor in Ringwood State Park. Garden admission is always free. It is open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. in daylight saving time and 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. in standard time.

Good to know: From Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day, weekends and holidays carry a cash parking fee of $5 for New Jersey cars. Free guided garden tours run Sundays from May through October. Your free State Parks Senior Citizen Pass covers park entrance fees. Garden details are on the Skylands website.

Where can I walk a long way on level ground?

Delaware and Raritan Canal towpath

The D&R Canal State Park has more than 70 miles of multi-use path beside a historic canal. A towpath follows the water, so grades are gentle. It suits walkers, cyclists and anyone pushing a wheelchair with help. Popular starting points include Bulls Island, the Prallsville Mills near Stockton, and Griggstown.

Before you go: The surface varies from section to section, so ask about the stretch you plan to walk. Pick a short out-and-back from a lot with restrooms. Walk 20 minutes out, then turn around. Call State Parks at 1-800-843-6420 to ask which lots have facilities open.

Island Beach State Park, Ocean County

A long barrier island of dunes, bay marsh and ocean beach, just south of Seaside Park. In fall and winter it is wonderfully empty. Bring your Senior Citizen Pass, which covers entrance. Ask at the gate which restrooms are open in the off-season and whether a beach wheelchair can be borrowed.

Cape May Point State Park and the Hawkwatch

Fall is the season here. New Jersey Audubon counts hawks from a platform just east of the state park parking lot, every day from September 1 to November 30, sunrise to sunset. Many of the best flights come in late September and October, often on northwest winds after a cold front.

The platform is a short walk from the car, and the counters are glad to point out birds. The lighthouse stands next to it. Nearby, the Cape May Bird Observatory's Northwood Center at 701 East Lake Drive is open daily, 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. It runs "E-Z Birding" walks at a relaxed pace, with no preregistration. Phone: 609-400-3868. Daily counts are posted on the Cape May Hawkwatch page.

Dress for wind. The platform is open to the weather, and a fleece and hat make a long sit far more pleasant.

What should I bring and watch for?

  1. Shoes with grip. Even paved paths have leaves and acorns in fall. Walking poles help on grass.
  2. A folding cane seat. Benches are not always where you need them. A lightweight seat lets you rest anywhere.
  3. Water and a snack. Cafés keep short hours in the off-season. The Farm Barn Café at Duke Farms, for example, keeps limited days, so check before you go.
  4. A plan for the restroom. Know the nearest one before you start, and use it before you set out.
  5. Your Senior Citizen Pass and a phone. Tell someone where you are going and when you expect to be back.
Common mistake

Trying to walk to the far end of a long path. Use the turn-around rule instead. When you have used half your energy, head back.

How do I make walking a habit?

Pick one place close to home and go every week for a month. You will learn where the benches are and how long the loop takes. Bring a friend, or join a guided tour like the Sunday walks at Skylands. For more ways to stay active, read our guide to healthy aging in New Jersey. For free ways to get out, see free and discounted things for NJ seniors and easy day trips.

Gardens change every week. The iris beds that look like grass in April are knee high and purple by Memorial Day. Going often is half the pleasure.

faq.q: Which New Jersey garden is best for a wheelchair?
faq.a: Duke Farms in Hillsborough has the most flat, paved trail, over 15 miles, plus a free accessibility transport you can reserve. Reeves-Reed Arboretum and the main paver path at Grounds For Sculpture are also good choices.

faq.q: When do the irises bloom at Presby in Montclair?
faq.a: Usually from mid-May through the first week of June. Check the garden's website each spring for its opening day.

faq.q: When are the Branch Brook Park cherry blossoms?
faq.a: Peak bloom usually comes in the second and third weeks of April, but it varies with the weather. In 2026 it ran from about April 3 to 12.

faq.q: Do seniors pay to enter New Jersey state parks?
faq.a: New Jersey residents 62 and older can get a free Senior Citizen Pass at any state park office. It covers entrance fees. Call 1-800-843-6420 for details.

faq.q: Can I see the Branch Brook Park cherry blossoms without walking?
faq.a: Yes. Essex County says you can drive through the park from one end to the other and see trees in bloom without getting out of the car. Parking along the park roads and at the Welcome Center lot is free.

faq.q: When is the Cape May hawk watch?
faq.a: New Jersey Audubon staffs the Cape May Hawkwatch platform at Cape May Point State Park every day from September 1 to November 30, sunrise to sunset. The platform is just east of the state park parking lot.

title: The Jersey Shore after Labor Day: a town-by-town guide
dek: Quiet beaches, easy parking and boardwalks you can actually stroll. Here is what stays open, where beach wheelchairs and mats are, and how to get there without driving.
keyFacts: Beaches in Atlantic City and Wildwood are free all year. Many other towns require beach tags only in summer.
Atlantic City has 175-foot beach access mats at Tallahassee, Bartram, Albany and Raleigh avenues.
Most beach wheelchair programs run with the summer lifeguards. Call ahead in the off-season.
NJ Transit offers reduced fares to riders 62 and older.
The Cape May Hawkwatch runs daily from September 1 to November 30.
body:
Ask anyone who lives at the Shore and they will tell you September and October are the best months. The water is still warm, the crowds are gone, and you can park near the boardwalk. Many restaurants and shops stay open on weekends well into fall.

There is one catch for anyone who needs help on sand. Most beach wheelchair programs are run by the beach patrol, and the lifeguards go home after the summer season. We checked each town's official information in October 2026. Below we tell you what we found and who to call.

After Labor Day the boardwalk belongs to the walkers, the dog owners and the people who brought a good book.

Monmouth County: which towns are easiest to reach by train?

NJ Transit's North Jersey Coast Line stops at Asbury Park, Spring Lake and Point Pleasant Beach. Riders 62 and older pay reduced fares. Have proof of age with you.

Ocean Grove

This Victorian camp meeting town is calm in any season, and it is even calmer now. Walk the boardwalk, then stroll past the tent cottages and the Great Auditorium. Check the Ocean Grove Camp Meeting Association calendar for organ concerts and holiday programs.

Accessibility: In summer, beach wheelchairs wait at the Webb Avenue, Embury Avenue, Ocean Pathway and Bath Avenue entrances, and staff push you down to the sand. In 2026 the guarded season ran daily through September 7. Ask the association whether chairs are available after that.

Good to know: Leashed dogs are allowed on the beach and boardwalk from September 15 to May 15.

Asbury Park

The boardwalk here runs past Convention Hall and the Stone Pony. In fall the calendar fills with weekend markets, like record shows and vintage sales. The train station is in town, and NJ Transit bus 317 runs from Philadelphia to the Asbury Park Transportation Center.

Spring Lake

Spring Lake is known for its quiet boardwalk and grand old houses. When the season ends, the borough closes its beach pavilions, pools and bathrooms, so plan your restroom stop in town. Badges are sold online during the season. Questions: Borough of Spring Lake, 732-449-0800.

Point Pleasant Beach

Jenkinson's Aquarium on the boardwalk is open daily, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Thanksgiving and Christmas. That makes it a dependable rainy-day stop. Seniors 65 and older pay $15 (adults $19). The aquarium's wheelchair lift is being replaced and is expected to be out of service until about November 30, so call 732-892-0600 first. Point Pleasant Beach has a train station, and NJ Transit bus 830 runs from Asbury Park station, with no Sunday service.

Ocean County and Atlantic City: what is open and accessible?

Long Beach Island

LBI in the fall is all lighthouse views, bay sunsets and empty beaches. Long Beach Township lends beach wheelchairs free to people staying at a township address. Chairs are delivered and picked up on Saturdays and reserved a week at a time. An attendant must push. Call the beach patrol at 609-361-1200 to ask about dates, or see the Beachwheels page. NJ Transit's shore page does not list LBI service, so plan to drive.

Atlantic City

Atlantic City is the most accessible beach town on this list in the off-season, and its beaches are free. Here is what the city's tourism office lists:

  • Beach mats: 175-foot access mats at the Tallahassee, Bartram, Albany and Raleigh Avenue entrances.
  • Ramps: Accessible ramps lead from the Boardwalk to the beach throughout the city.
  • Surf chairs: Lent first come, first served by the Beach Patrol at Mississippi Avenue. Call 609-347-5307 to check.
  • Year-round restrooms: At New York, Mississippi and Chelsea avenues on the Boardwalk.

Details are on the Atlantic City access page.

Getting there by transit: The Atlantic City Rail Line runs daily from Philadelphia's 30th Street Station to the Atlantic City Rail Terminal, a few blocks from the Boardwalk. From North Jersey, NJ Transit bus 319 runs express from Port Authority with stops at Newark Penn Station and Journal Square. Bus 551 runs from Philadelphia. Bus 319 excursion tickets are sold through the NJ Transit mobile app or at the Port Authority Bus Terminal, so buy before you board.

Cape May County: what do the southern towns offer?

Ocean City

Ocean City's boardwalk runs about 2.5 miles. The local chamber says many restaurants, arcades and shops stay open through the off-season, which it counts from November to March. The Music Pier hosts concerts into the fall.

Accessibility: Ocean City runs a free surf chair program from the 46th Street Information Center, 46th Street and West Avenue, open 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Chairs can be borrowed for a day or up to a week. Call 609-554-0352 for information or reservations. For the boardwalk itself, the city lends a few regular wheelchairs free, two hours at a time, from the Music Pier Information Center between 8th and 9th streets. Call 609-399-6111 ext. 9337. Accessible restrooms are at 1st, 6th, 10th, 11th and 12th streets, the Music Pier, the 34th Street playground and the 58th Street beach. Shaded boardwalk pavilions near 8th through 12th streets are a good place to sit. Ask which restrooms stay open after the summer.

The Wildwoods

Wildwood's beach is wide and free. The city says ADA beach wheelchairs are available, plus a beach taxi from four pickup points. The taxi runs Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day weekend, 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Accessible paths under the boardwalk are at East Bennett, East Spicer and East Maple avenues. To arrange help, call 609-846-2012. NJ Transit buses 313 and 315 serve Wildwood and Cape May all year.

Cape May

Fall may be Cape May's finest season. Since 2024 the city has laid about two miles of ADA beach mats, running parallel to the ocean from Madison Avenue at the east end of the promenade to the Cove at Third Avenue, with platforms that reach toward the water. The city also keeps 12 beach wheelchairs at entrances along the beachfront, first come, first served, from 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. To make special arrangements, call the Cape May Beach Patrol at 609-884-9520. Beach tags are required only from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day. In summer, free public restrooms sit about every half mile along the promenade, so ask which stay open in fall. Leashed dogs are allowed on Cape May city beaches and the promenade from September 15 to May 15, so expect some furry company.

Cape May MAC runs fall and holiday programs, including Victorian Weekend, Halloween Happenings and Christmas in Cape May. Its Historic District trolley tour runs all year, and one trolley has a wheelchair lift. Reserve it two weeks ahead at 609-884-5404. The lighthouse has 199 steps and no elevator, but the oil house exhibit at its base is accessible.

Should I drive or take the train?

Driving gives you the most freedom, and fall parking is far easier than in July. Parking rules differ from town to town, and some meters run all year, so read the signs before you walk away. If you have a disability placard, bring it. Accessible spaces near boardwalk ramps fill first on sunny weekends.

The train is a relaxing choice for Monmouth County towns. The North Jersey Coast Line reaches Asbury Park, Spring Lake and Point Pleasant Beach. Ask how far the station is from where you want to go, and line up a taxi or ride if the walk is long. For Atlantic City, the train and the 319 bus both end near the Boardwalk. Check schedules on the NJ Transit Jersey Shore page before you leave, since fall timetables are thinner than summer ones.

What happens at the Shore every fall?

  • Hawk migration at Cape May Point. New Jersey Audubon counts hawks from a platform beside the state park lot every day from September 1 to November 30. Many of the best flights come in late September and October.
  • The Cape May Fall Festival. New Jersey Audubon's birding festival is held each October, with many events in and around Cape May. In 2026 it ran October 15 to 18. Its Northwood Center also runs relaxed "E-Z Birding" walks.
  • Halloween and holiday programs. Cape May MAC's Halloween and Christmas events return each year. Ocean City's long-running Halloween Parade travels Asbury Avenue downtown. In 2026 it stepped off October 29 at 7:15 p.m.
  • Weekend markets and races. Asbury Park's boardwalk hosts markets. The Atlantic City Marathon weekend is held in mid-October (October 17 and 18 in 2026), so expect road closures and busy hotels that weekend.

Check each organizer's website for this year's dates before you go.

How do I plan an easy off-season Shore day?

  1. Pick one town. Shore traffic is light in fall, but the Garden State Parkway still adds up. One town and one meal makes a good day.
  2. Call about access the week before. Ask whether beach wheelchairs or mats are still out, and which restrooms are open.
  3. Check the weather and the wind. A sunny 60-degree day on the boardwalk can feel much colder by the water. Bring a windbreaker and a hat.
  4. Go midweek if you can. Some businesses cut back to weekends in the fall, so check restaurant hours first. The upside is easy parking.
  5. Use your senior fare. If you take NJ Transit, show proof of age for the reduced fare. Your free State Parks Senior Citizen Pass covers park entrance, including Cape May Point and Island Beach.
Common mistake

Assuming summer services still run. Lifeguards, beach taxis and many surf chair programs stop after Labor Day. One phone call saves a long walk on soft sand.

What if sand is too hard for me?

You can still have a wonderful day. Sit on a boardwalk bench and watch the surf. Ride a Cape May trolley with a lift. Visit the Jenkinson's aquarium once its lift is back in service. In Atlantic City, roll down a ramp and out along a beach mat. A boardwalk lunch with a view counts as a Shore day too.

For more outings, see our list of easy day trips in New Jersey and our guide to free and discounted things for NJ seniors. If you are going with grandchildren, see our guide to days out with the grandkids.

faq.q: Are New Jersey beaches free after Labor Day?
faq.a: Many towns only require beach tags during the summer guarded season. Cape May, for example, requires them from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day. Atlantic City and Wildwood beaches are free all year.

faq.q: Can I get a beach wheelchair at the Shore in the fall?
faq.a: Possibly, but call first. Most programs are run by the beach patrol in summer. Atlantic City lends surf chairs at Mississippi Avenue (609-347-5307), and Cape May's Beach Patrol lends free chairs (609-884-9520).

faq.q: Which Shore town has beach mats for wheelchairs?
faq.a: Atlantic City has 175-foot access mats at the Tallahassee, Bartram, Albany and Raleigh Avenue entrances, plus ramps from the Boardwalk.

faq.q: Can I get to the Shore without a car?
faq.a: Yes. The North Jersey Coast Line serves Asbury Park, Spring Lake and Point Pleasant Beach. The Atlantic City Rail Line and bus 319 reach Atlantic City. Buses 313 and 315 serve Wildwood and Cape May all year. Riders 62 and older pay reduced fares.

faq.q: Does Ocean City lend beach wheelchairs?
faq.a: Yes. Ocean City's free surf chair program operates from the 46th Street Information Center, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., for a day or up to a week. Call 609-554-0352. A few regular wheelchairs for the boardwalk can be borrowed at the Music Pier Information Center.

faq.q: Are dogs allowed on New Jersey beaches in the fall?
faq.a: In some towns. Ocean Grove allows leashed dogs on the beach and boardwalk from September 15 to May 15, and Cape May city beaches allow leashed dogs from September 15 to May 15. Rules differ by town, so check before you go.

title: Free beach wheelchairs and accessible beaches in NJ
dek: Where to borrow a free beach wheelchair at the Jersey Shore, which towns lay mats toward the water, where the accessible restrooms are, and how to plan a beach day for a parent with a walker.
keyFacts: Many Jersey Shore towns lend beach wheelchairs free. Someone else must push them; the rider can't move them alone.
New Jersey's lifeguarded state park beaches have beach mats and wheelchairs. Island Beach State Park keeps chairs at the park office outside swimming season: 732-793-0506.
Sandy Hook has beach wheelchairs through the Visitor Center at 732-872-5970, and accessible restrooms at all six beach centers.
Avalon and Surf City list beach wheelchairs as available all year. Most other town programs run only with the summer lifeguards.
NJ residents 62 and older can get a free State Parks Senior Citizen Pass for park entrance.
body:
You can get your mom or dad onto the sand at the Jersey Shore even if they can't walk on it. Many shore towns lend beach wheelchairs for free, with big balloon wheels that roll over soft sand. A family member or a lifeguard pushes the chair. Several towns also lay firm mats from the boardwalk toward the water, which help a person using a walker or cane as much as a wheelchair user.

Each program has its own rules. Some take reservations, some are first come, first served, and some only lend to people staying in town. We checked each town's or park's own page in fall 2026. Most programs run only with the summer lifeguards, roughly Memorial Day to Labor Day, and details can change from year to year, so call before you go.

How do free beach wheelchairs work?

You sign one out from the beach patrol, the beach office or the recreation department, usually with a photo ID. It's free, but someone has to push it, and you must return it by closing time unless you reserved it for longer.

Know these limits before you plan:

  • They need a pusher. Long Beach Township, Ship Bottom and Surf City all say the rider can't move the chair alone. Sea Isle City requires an attendant 16 or older.
  • Weight limits. Avalon and Sea Isle City list a maximum of 250 pounds.
  • They don't fold. Avalon and Sea Isle City forbid tying one to a car roof, and Surf City says you need a pickup truck or large SUV to move one.
  • Shallow water only. Avalon says not deeper than six inches. Sea Isle City says about six inches, with the attendant right there.
  • They stay in town. Most programs forbid taking chairs to another beach.
Ask for the chair by phone before you load the car. Most towns have only a handful.

Which state and federal beaches have beach wheelchairs?

NJ State Parks says its lifeguarded beaches have beach mats and wheelchairs. Island Beach State Park and Sandy Hook are the two big ocean choices.

Island Beach State Park, Seaside Park. Beach wheelchairs for the swimming area, plus chairs fitted for surf fishing, wait at the bathing pavilions in swimming season and at the park office the rest of the year. The Fisherman's Walkway at parking area 7 is a boardwalk from ocean to bay. Call the park office at 732-793-0506. When we checked in November 2026, the park's page said the Fisherman's Walkway restrooms were closed for repairs, with restrooms open at the swimming area pavilion and areas 13, 19 and 21. Check the park page for current notices before you go. Your free State Parks Senior Citizen Pass covers entrance.

The state park beaches also include lakes inland, such as Cheesequake, Hopatcong, Swartswood, Wawayanda and Round Valley. For help with a wheelchair at any of them, call the park office or the State Parks office in Trenton at 609-984-0370.

Sandy Hook, Gateway National Recreation Area. The National Park Service says beach wheelchairs are available through the Visitor Center at 732-872-5970. Restrooms at all six beach centers (Areas B, C, D, E, Gunnison and North Beach) are wheelchair accessible, all parking lots have accessible spaces, and the five-mile Multi-Use Pathway and the North Beach Observation Deck are accessible.

Where can I borrow a beach wheelchair in Monmouth County?

Asbury Park, Belmar and Ocean Grove all have chairs at the beach entrances in summer. You ask at the entrance rather than reserving weeks ahead.

Asbury Park. The city has a limited number of beach wheelchairs. Ask at any ticket booth. It also has a few WaterWheels adaptive chairs. See the city's beach page for details. Every beach entrance has a ramp to the sand and mobile beach mats, and every block has accessible parking and curb cuts. Metered spaces marked for people with disabilities are free. Visitors 62 and older paid $20 for a senior season badge in 2026. The Convention Hall restrooms are open 6 a.m. to midnight all year. Beach Office: 732-502-8863.

Belmar. Beach wheelchairs are at every avenue entrance except 3rd, 13th, 17th and 21st. Accessible bathrooms are at 3rd, 6th, 8th, 11th, 16th and 19th Avenues. Each avenue has one accessible parking space and a curb cut and ramp. The Beach Department is at 732-749-4530 in season.

Ocean Grove. No reservation is needed in season. Beach wheelchairs wait at the Webb Avenue, Embury Avenue, Ocean Pathway and Bath Avenue entrances. Tell the attendant, and a lifeguard or staff member will push your parent to the beach and help them into their own beach chair. When it's time to go, the lifeguards bring the wheelchair back. In summer 2026, lifeguards worked daily from June 19 to September 7.

What about Long Beach Island?

LBI towns lend chairs, but several limit them to people staying in that town. Reserve early.

  • Long Beach Township. Its Beachwheels program lends free chairs to anyone staying at a township address, not hotels unless arranged ahead. Reservations open as early as January and run Saturday to Saturday. Chairs are delivered and picked up. Beach Patrol: 609-361-1200.
  • Ship Bottom. Free for anyone staying in Ship Bottom, by reservation, up to one week. Call 609-494-9481 in season or 609-494-2171 ext. 116 off-season. Hotel guests need arrangements made ahead. Mobi-mats are on most streets. A free beach taxi for people with physical challenges runs from Father's Day weekend to Labor Day.
  • Surf City. Beach wheelchairs are available all year, first come, first served, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., at the badge booth, at no cost. They can't be delivered. When the beaches are guarded, the borough's Gator vehicles carry people with an ADA Gator badge over the dune and along the dune fence. North 12th Street is the designated accessible entrance. Badge booth: 609-361-7655. Surf City requires badges only for ages 12 to 64, so a parent 65 or older goes free.

Which South Jersey beaches have mats and chairs?

Atlantic City, Ocean City and Cape May have the most mats and chairs. Avalon lends chairs all year, and Sea Isle City takes reservations off-season.

TownChairsCall
Atlantic CityFirst come609-347-5307
Ocean CityDay or week609-554-0352
Sea Isle CityReserve609-263-0050
AvalonAll year609-967-7587
WildwoodSummer609-846-2012
Cape MayFirst come609-884-9520
  • Atlantic City. The beaches are free. There are 175-foot mats at Tallahassee, Bartram, Albany and Raleigh avenues. Surf chairs come from the Beach Patrol at Mississippi Avenue. Restrooms at New York, Mississippi and Chelsea avenues stay open all year.
  • Ocean City. Free surf chairs at the 46th Street Information Center, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., for a day or up to a week. Lifeguard headquarters on 1st, 12th, 34th and 58th streets have chairs for a quick trip onto the sand. The Music Pier lends boardwalk wheelchairs for two hours, 609-399-6111 ext. 9337. All boardwalk and beach restrooms are accessible.
  • Sea Isle City. Free chairs from the Recreation Department, picked up at the Community Center, 4500 Central Avenue. Reservations are taken in and out of season, for up to seven days in a row. Bring two IDs, or one photo ID.
  • Avalon. Free surf chairs all year, first come, first served, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. at 9th, 30th and 80th streets and 32nd and Avalon Avenue. Off-season, ask at Community Hall, 609-967-3066. In summer 2026, mats were at 13 street ends.
  • Wildwood. Beach wheelchairs and a beach taxi, 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day weekend. Accessible paths under the boardwalk at East Bennett, East Spicer and East Maple avenues.
  • Cape May. About two miles of ADA mats from Madison Avenue to the Cove, with platforms toward the water. Twelve beach wheelchairs, first come, first served, 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Ocean City reminds drivers that a disability placard does not mean free meters. Under state law you pay the meter, and filling it to the maximum then covers up to 24 hours. Our placard guide explains how to apply.

How do I plan a beach day for a parent with a walker?

Pick a town with mats, park close to a ramp, and set up near the end of the mat. A walker sinks in soft sand, so let the mat or a beach wheelchair do the work.

  1. Call ahead. Ask how many chairs they have, whether to reserve, which entrance has the mat and the nearest accessible restroom.
  2. Go early on a weekday. Accessible spaces near the ramps fill first, and chairs go fast on sunny weekends.
  3. Bring two pushers if you can. Pushing a loaded chair through deep sand is hard. One person can steady the chair while the other pulls.
  4. Leave the walker at the mat's end or bring it in the chair's lap, so your parent has support standing up to go home.
  5. Plan for the sun. Bring an umbrella, a hat, water and a beach chair with arms. Some beach wheelchairs come with an umbrella. Our heat safety guide lists warning signs to watch for.
  6. Know the restroom distance. A long walk to the bathroom ends many beach days early. Set up near one.
If sand is too much today

A boardwalk bench with an ocean view is a fine outing too. Ocean City's shaded pavilions near 8th through 12th streets, Sandy Hook's paved pathway and the Island Beach Fisherman's Walkway all give a parent the sea air without the sand.

Have your parent wear shoes with grip on the mat and take it slowly. Our guide to preventing falls has more.

Can we use a beach wheelchair in the off-season?

Sometimes. Avalon, Surf City and Island Beach State Park list chairs outside summer, and Sea Isle City takes off-season reservations. Most other programs end with the lifeguards after Labor Day.

For a quieter fall or spring visit, see our Jersey Shore after Labor Day guide, and for more outings, our easy day trips and our list of places to take the grandkids.

faq.q: How do I get my dad onto the beach if he uses a wheelchair?
faq.a: Borrow a free beach wheelchair from the town's beach patrol or recreation office and push him over the sand, or use a town with beach mats from the boardwalk. Call ahead, since many towns have only a few chairs and some take reservations.

faq.q: Are beach wheelchairs free in New Jersey?
faq.a: At the towns and parks in this guide, yes. You may need ID, and some towns, including Sea Isle City and Avalon, hold the person who signs it out responsible for damage.

faq.q: Can my mom push her own beach wheelchair?
faq.a: No. Programs like Long Beach Township, Ship Bottom and Surf City say an attendant must move the chair. Sea Isle City requires an attendant 16 or older.

faq.q: Do I need a reservation for a beach wheelchair?
faq.a: It depends on the town. Long Beach Township and Ship Bottom require reservations. Atlantic City, Cape May, Avalon and Surf City lend chairs first come, first served. Ocean Grove needs no reservation. Ocean City takes reservations, and Sea Isle City recommends reserving early.

faq.q: Can I take a beach wheelchair to another town?
faq.a: Usually not. Most programs say chairs must stay on that town's beaches. Avalon's can't leave Seven Mile Island.

faq.q: Which NJ beach is easiest for someone using a walker?
faq.a: Look for long mats and nearby accessible restrooms. Cape May has about two miles of mats, Atlantic City has 175-foot mats at four entrances, and Asbury Park has mats at every entrance. Call to confirm mats are out before you go.

title: Senior fishing in NJ: free license at 70 and easy places to fish
dek: New Jersey residents 70 and older fish fresh water free, and 65 to 69 pay a senior rate. Here is how the saltwater registry works, when Free Fishing Days fall, and where to fish from railed walkways and accessible docks.
keyFacts: NJ residents 70 and older need no freshwater fishing license and no trout stamp.
Residents 65 to 69 pay $12.50 for a senior resident license; licenses run through December 31.
There is no saltwater license, but anglers 16 and older must register each year with the free NJ Saltwater Recreational Registry.
NJ Fish and Wildlife holds two Free Fishing Days a year, in June and September.
Barnegat Lighthouse State Park has a 1,033-foot railed concrete walkway on the south jetty for anglers with disabilities.
body:
New Jersey residents age 70 and older can fish the state's fresh waters for free. They need no fishing license and no trout stamp. Residents 65 to 69 pay a discounted senior license of $12.50 a year. In salt water there is no license at all, but every angler 16 and older must sign up each year for the free New Jersey Saltwater Recreational Registry.

That makes fishing one of the cheapest outdoor hobbies an older adult can pick back up. If your mom or dad fished years ago and stopped, the hardest part is usually getting there and finding a spot that is safe underfoot. This guide covers the rules, the places with railings, docks and paved walkways, and how to plan an easy first morning out.

Do seniors need a fishing license in New Jersey?

It depends on age and on the kind of water, fresh or salt. Residents 70 and over fish fresh water free. Residents 65 to 69 buy a lower priced senior license.

WhoFresh water rule (2026)
Residents 16 to 64Resident fishing license, $22.50
Residents 65 to 69Senior resident license, $12.50
Residents 70 and olderFree. No license and no trout stamp needed
Trout and salmon, residents 16 to 69Trout stamp also required, $10.50
Under 16No license needed

Licenses and trout stamps run from the date you buy them through December 31. To get the resident rate, you must have lived in New Jersey for at least the previous six months. NJ Fish and Wildlife says the license must be displayed on outer clothing, so a clip-on holder helps.

Your parent needs the trout stamp only for trout or salmon, and they need it even if they release every fish. At 70 and over, the stamp goes away along with the license. Rules on size, season and how many fish you can keep still apply at every age.

You can buy a license online through NJ Fish and Wildlife or at a license agent, which includes many bait and tackle shops. For trouble buying or printing a license, call the state's licensing vendor, Aspira, at 888-773-8450. To fix a customer profile, call NJ Fish and Wildlife at 609-940-4350.

At 70, the license and the trout stamp both go away. The fish limits do not.

What about saltwater fishing at the Shore?

New Jersey has no saltwater fishing license. Anglers 16 and older must register each year with the free New Jersey Saltwater Recreational Registry Program, and that includes older adults.

Registration covers fishing with a rod or hand line in marine waters and in fresh tidal waters. The state says the registry is not a license. It replaced a federal registry and its fee for people who fish in New Jersey. You are exempt if you fish only from a party or charter boat that is itself registered with the program. Ask the captain when you book.

Shellfish are different. Clamming needs its own license. Island Beach State Park, for example, notes that a clamming license is required in the Sedge Islands area and that clamming is not allowed on Sundays. Older adults get a break here. Residents 62 and older can get a free lifetime senior shellfish license, with a $2 application fee.

Is there a free fishing day in New Jersey?

Yes. NJ Fish and Wildlife holds two Free Fishing Days a year, one in June and one in September. On those days, residents can fish the state's public waters without a license or trout stamp. Size and catch limits still apply.

In 2026 they fell on Saturday, June 6, and Saturday, September 26. The June date lines up with National Fishing and Boating Week and the September date with National Hunting and Fishing Day. Watch the Fish and Wildlife Free Fishing Days page for the 2027 dates. These days matter most for a parent aged 65 to 69 who wants to try fishing again before paying for a license, or for a younger family member who comes along to help.

What about helping? The state's rule is written for children. Baiting a hook, netting a fish or unhooking it for a child needs no license, but casting, reeling in or fighting the fish does. Fish and Wildlife does not spell out a rule for helping another adult, so if you plan to do more than bait and net for your mom or dad, buy your own license, unless you are 70 or older too.

Another option for a returning angler is the Fishing Buddy License. A new angler buying with a returning angler, or two new anglers buying together, can each save nearly 50 percent.

Where can older adults fish without climbing over rocks?

NJ Fish and Wildlife keeps a list of more than 50 fishing sites for people who have trouble with mobility. Some have docks built for wheelchairs, and others have paved paths or level shoreline you can drive close to. Call the site before you go, because conditions change.

A few that are well described on state pages:

  • Barnegat Lighthouse State Park, Barnegat Light. A 1,033-foot concrete walkway with handrails runs along the top of the south jetty and gives anglers with disabilities access to Barnegat Inlet. The picnic area is also accessible. There is no entrance fee. Park office: 609-494-2016. Pets are not allowed on the jetty walkway.
  • Island Beach State Park, Seaside Park. The Fisherman's Walkway at parking Area 7 is a boardwalk to both the ocean and the bay. The park has beach wheelchairs specially fitted for surf fishing, at the pavilions in summer and at the park office the rest of the year. As of this writing, the park lists the restrooms at the Fisherman's Walkway (Areas 6 and 7) as closed for repairs, with others open at the swimming pavilion and Areas 13, 19 and 21. Park office: 732-793-0506.
  • Shark River Access, Avon-by-the-Sea. This one-acre state Wildlife Management Area sits on the north side of Shark River Inlet, under the bridge, with ample parking. Anglers catch winter and summer flounder, blowfish, tautog, bluefish and striped bass. The state notes the jetty rocks are slippery and suggests studded footwear for anyone who goes out on them. For an older adult, the edge of the inlet is the safer spot.

Inland, the state's accessible sites list includes places like the wheelchair dock at Echo Lake Park in Mountainside, the accessible floating dock at Lake Aeroflex in Kittatinny Valley State Park, two accessible fishing docks at Wawayanda State Park, and an ADA boat dock at Atsion Lake in Wharton State Forest. The state's list was last updated in 2006, so treat it as a starting point and call the park first. The State Park Service's general accessibility line is 609-984-0370.

For more places with benches and restrooms nearby, see our guide to New Jersey gardens and easy walks, and for Shore towns in the cooler months, the Jersey Shore after Labor Day.

How can a senior save money on a fishing trip?

Start with the free state parks pass. New Jersey residents 62 and older can get a free Senior Citizen Pass at any state park office, which covers entrance fees where they are charged. Island Beach, for example, charges an entrance fee in season and off season.

Other savings to know about:

  • Residents 70 and older do not need the $15 Boat Ramp Permit that some Wildlife Management Area ramps require.
  • Totally blind residents can get a free fishing license. Call 609-940-4350 for an application.
  • Veterans with a service-connected disability of any degree can get free licenses once NJ Fish and Wildlife certifies them. Call 609-940-4350 to start. Our guide to benefits for older veterans has more on state veteran programs.
  • A disability placard helps at busy lots. See how to get a parking placard.

Our list of free and discounted things to do after 60 rounds up more state park and museum savings.

How do I take my mom or dad fishing safely?

Pick a spot with railings or a dock, go in the morning, and keep the trip short. Two hours with a snack and a restroom nearby beats a long day on wet rocks.

  1. Call the park office. Ask where the accessible fishing area is, where the nearest open restroom is, and whether a beach wheelchair is available that day.
  2. Handle the paperwork at home. Buy the license or register for the saltwater registry online before you go. If your parent is 70 or older, the state says a driver's license or other ID with date of birth serves as their license, so bring it.
  3. Pack light and sit down. A folding chair with arms, a hat, sunscreen, water and a small cart make a big difference. Leave the tackle box at home and bring only what you will use.
  4. Watch the footing. Jetties, docks and bulkheads get slick. State pages warn about slippery rocks at inlets. Wear shoes with good grip, and stay on walkways. Our guide to preventing falls has more on balance and footwear.
  5. Mind the weather and the hands. Hooks and cold, wet fingers do not mix. Pre-tied rigs and long-nose pliers make baiting and unhooking easier for stiff or arthritic hands.
  6. Check before you eat the catch. NJDEP and the NJ Department of Health publish fish consumption advisories by species and location. Look them up before cooking anything you keep.

If your parent no longer drives, a fishing morning can also be a reason to see a grandchild. It also pairs well with a picnic at a state park, and you will find more outing ideas in our easy day trips around New Jersey.

Are there fishing classes or programs for beginners?

Yes. NJ Fish and Wildlife runs fishing education programs and lists them on its events calendar, from beginner basics to more advanced skills. Its "Great Fishing Close to Home" app helps you search for nearby waters by location or species.

You can email the state's fishing education staff at njfishingr3@dep.nj.gov with questions. Local senior centers, county parks and sportsmen's clubs sometimes run casual fishing outings too. Your county's senior services office can tell you what is on the calendar; start from our county pages.

Before you go

Fees, Free Fishing Day dates and park advisories change. Check the NJ Fish and Wildlife license page and the park's own page the week of your trip, or call the park office.

faq.q: At what age is fishing free in New Jersey?
faq.a: New Jersey residents 70 and older do not need a freshwater fishing license or a trout stamp. Residents 65 to 69 can buy a discounted senior license for $12.50. Saltwater anglers 16 and older of any age must still register for the free NJ Saltwater Recreational Registry each year.

faq.q: Does my 72-year-old dad need to register to fish at the Jersey Shore?
faq.a: Yes. New Jersey has no saltwater license, but every angler 16 and older must register each year with the free NJ Saltwater Recreational Registry. The only exception is fishing solely from a party or charter boat that is registered with the program.

faq.q: Do I need a license to help my mom fish?
faq.a: NJ Fish and Wildlife's rule is written for helping a child: baiting a hook, netting a fish or unhooking it needs no license, but casting, reeling in or fighting the fish does. The state does not spell out a rule for helping another adult, so if you will do more than bait and net, buy your own license unless you are 70 or older.

faq.q: Where can someone in a wheelchair fish in New Jersey?
faq.a: NJ Fish and Wildlife keeps a list of more than 50 accessible fishing sites. Examples include the railed concrete walkway on the south jetty at Barnegat Lighthouse State Park and the Fisherman's Walkway at Island Beach State Park, which also has beach wheelchairs fitted for surf fishing. Call the park office before you go.

faq.q: When are New Jersey's Free Fishing Days?
faq.a: NJ Fish and Wildlife holds one in June and one in September. In 2026 they were June 6 and September 26. Residents can fish public waters those days without a license or trout stamp. Check the Fish and Wildlife website for 2027 dates.

faq.q: Do seniors need a trout stamp in NJ?
faq.a: Residents 16 to 69 need a trout stamp, $10.50, to fish for or keep trout or salmon, even if they release them. Residents 70 and older do not need one.

title: Scenic drives in NJ for seniors who can't walk far
dek: Wildlife from the car window, river roads, cliff-top lookouts and Pine Barrens byways, with the restroom stops and passes that make an easy afternoon.
keyFacts: Forsythe Refuge's Wildlife Drive is 8 miles, open sunrise to sunset, and costs $4 per car.
National wildlife refuges, Forsythe included, waive entrance fees on several fee-free days each year, including Veterans Day.
New Jersey has eight designated scenic byways, each marked with its own road signs.
State Line Lookout on the Palisades has restrooms and an accessible cafe. The other two lookouts have none.
High Point State Park entrance is free from Labor Day to Memorial Day weekend.
body:
Some of the prettiest places in New Jersey can be seen without leaving the car. The Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge has an 8-mile Wildlife Drive through salt marsh. Route 29 follows the Delaware River from Trenton to Frenchtown. The Palisades Interstate Parkway has pull-off lookouts high above the Hudson, and the state's designated scenic byways wind through the Pine Barrens, farm country and the Highlands.

These drives are a good fit for a mom or dad who can no longer walk far but still loves to get out. Below are the best routes, where the restrooms are, and how to plan a comfortable afternoon. For places where you get out and walk a bit, see our 20 easy day trips.

Which New Jersey drives are best when walking is hard?

Start with the Forsythe Wildlife Drive, the Palisades lookouts and Route 29 along the Delaware. All three let you enjoy the view through the windshield and have restrooms you can plan around.

New Jersey has eight designated scenic byways, according to the New Jersey Department of Transportation. Each has its own road signs with a byway logo. Six are also National Scenic Byways. Lengths below come from the official NJ Scenic Byways site and are approximate.

You do not need to drive a whole byway. Pick a 30 to 60 minute piece, plan one stop with a restroom and a place to eat, and head home while everyone is still in a good mood.

What is the Forsythe Wildlife Drive like from the car?

It is an 8-mile, self-guided auto tour through salt marsh, freshwater pools and upland forest near Atlantic City. You can see herons, egrets, ducks and hawks without opening the door.

The drive starts at refuge headquarters, 800 Great Creek Road in Oceanville, at the end of Great Creek Road off Route 9. The gate opens at sunrise and closes at sunset, every day of the year. Numbered "Blue Goose" signs along the route match a free self-guided tour pamphlet you can download from the refuge website, so a passenger can read aloud about each stop.

  • Cost. $4 per car. The refuge honors America the Beautiful passes. A lifetime Senior Pass for U.S. citizens or residents 62 and older costs $80, and an annual Senior Pass costs $20.
  • Buying a pass. The Visitor Information Center is open Wednesday to Sunday, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., closed holidays. Pass sales there are cash or check only.
  • Free days. National wildlife refuges waive the entrance fee on several days a year, including Veterans Day. The refuge website lists the current dates.
  • Restrooms. Accessible restrooms are at the headquarters area. Go before you start the loop.
  • If someone wants to stretch. Observation towers stand at Gull Pond and Turtle Cove. Your parent can stay in the car while you climb.

Call the refuge at 609-652-1665 with questions. The refuge's website links to tide information for the drive, and bird activity often changes with the tide. Pack bug spray from late spring to early fall.

A passenger with binoculars in the front seat sees as much of Forsythe as anyone on foot.

Where can you drive along the Delaware River?

Route 29, the Delaware River Scenic Byway, runs about 34 miles from Trenton north to Frenchtown, with the river and the Delaware and Raritan Canal beside you much of the way. Farther north, Old Mine Road threads through the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area.

Route 29, Trenton to Frenchtown

The byway passes Washington Crossing State Park, Titusville, Lambertville, Stockton, Raven Rock and Frenchtown. The canal towpath is visible along the whole route. Lambertville, Stockton and Frenchtown all have places to eat in town, which makes a natural turnaround point.

Restrooms on the byway's official list include Washington Crossing State Park, Prallsville Mills in Stockton, and the Lambertville access area next to the Lambertville Station restaurant. The Kingwood boat access restroom is open in summer only.

Old Mine Road, Delaware Water Gap

The National Park Service calls Old Mine Road one of the oldest commercial roads in the country, built in the mid-1600s. Today it links historic stops like Millbrook Village, Walpack Center and Peters Valley, and several buildings open only on summer weekends.

Check before you go. Parts of Old Mine Road have been closed for repaving and slowed by bridge work, and Route 615 between Flatbrookville and Pompey Ridge has been closed by a landslide. The park posts current closures on its conditions page. Restrooms are few and far apart here, so this is a better drive for a parent who does not need frequent stops. The park's phone number is 570-426-2452.

Where are the best views without hiking in North Jersey?

The Palisades Interstate Parkway lookouts and High Point State Park both give big views from the parking area. The Western Highlands byway adds farm valleys and mountain scenery in Sussex County.

Palisades Interstate Parkway lookouts

About 11 miles of the parkway run through New Jersey, from the George Washington Bridge to the New York line at Alpine. Only passenger cars and motorcycles are allowed. The Palisades Interstate Park Commission lists three lookouts:

  • Rockefeller Lookout, Englewood Cliffs, about 1 mile north of Exit 1. Northbound only. Open 24 hours. No restrooms.
  • Alpine Lookout, about 3 miles north of Exit 1. Northbound only. Open 24 hours. No restrooms.
  • State Line Lookout, 2 miles north of Exit 2, with its own exit from the northbound side and a U-turn from the southbound side. At 520 feet, it is the highest point on the Palisades cliffs. Parking is metered year round. The State Line Cafe, built in 1937, is fully accessible, has restrooms and is open about 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. most days. The cafe's number is 201-750-0465.

Drive northbound to reach all three. State Line Lookout may close during a big winter storm.

High Point State Park, Wantage

High Point is the highest spot in New Jersey at 1,803 feet. From the ridge you can see the Poconos, the Catskills and the Wallkill River Valley. The 220-foot monument honors New Jersey's veterans, which can make this a meaningful drive for a parent who served. See our guide to benefits for older veterans.

Entrance is free from Labor Day to Memorial Day weekend. The gate is open 8 a.m. to sunset from April 1 to November 30, and 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. from December 1 to March 31. Winter access to the monument area depends on road conditions. The park says its facilities are partially accessible, so call the park office at 973-875-4800 to ask where to park closest to the views. The Interpretive Center is accessible.

Western Highlands Scenic Byway, Sussex County

This roughly 23-mile byway around Vernon passes old farms, Wawayanda State Park and the Wallkill River National Wildlife Refuge. Wawayanda State Park is the most reliable restroom stop.

Is there a scenic drive through the Pine Barrens?

Yes. The Pine Barrens Scenic Byway, a National Scenic Byway since 2021, covers about 130 miles of quiet roads through pine forest, cedar rivers and old villages in Atlantic, Burlington, Cape May, Cumberland and Ocean counties.

The route runs from Batsto and Tuckerton in the north to Dennisville and Port Elizabeth in the south. Long stretches have no gas stations or stores, so fill the tank and pack water and snacks before you head in. Good stops with restrooms include Batsto Village in Wharton State Forest, Tuckerton Seaport, Historic Smithville in Galloway, and Belleplain State Forest. The byway also passes the Forsythe refuge, so you can pair the two in one day.

The Pinelands Commission has an interactive story map of the byway that a family member can pull up on a tablet in the passenger seat. Our day trips guide covers Batsto Village in more detail.

Farther west, the Bayshore Heritage Byway runs about 122 miles along the Delaware Bay through Salem, Cumberland and Cape May counties, past marshes, small fishing towns and farm fields. It ends at Cape May Point, where the byway notes comfort stations along the beachfront are open year round. For the coast itself, see our Jersey Shore off-season guide.

Where should we drive for fall color, or any season?

For leaves, start in the higher hills of North Jersey, where color usually comes first, then work south as the season goes on. High Point, the Western Highlands byway and Old Mine Road are good fall picks. The Pine Barrens and the Delaware Bay roads tend to hold color later.

Two shorter byways are pleasant in any season:

  • Millstone Valley Scenic Byway. About 25 miles along the Millstone River and the Delaware and Raritan Canal, past old Dutch villages, lock houses and Rockingham, Washington's last wartime headquarters. The byway visitor center in the Griggstown Bridgetender's House is open Saturdays and Sundays, 1 to 4 p.m., April through October. Restrooms at Kingston Lock are open May to October.
  • Upper Freehold Historic Farmland Byway. About 28 miles of country roads in western Monmouth County, with farms worked by the same families for generations. Allentown's historic district has shops and cafes. Historic Walnford, with its gristmill, has restrooms.

In winter, bare trees open up river and valley views you cannot see in summer. Just check the forecast, keep a blanket in the back seat and skip the drive if roads are icy.

How do I plan a drive for a parent who can't walk far?

Keep it short, plan the restroom stops in advance and bring the passes and placard that make parking easy. A two-hour outing that ends on a high note beats an all-day trip that wears everyone out.

  1. Check conditions the morning of. Look at 511nj.org for traffic and closures, and the park's own page for road work.
  2. Map your restrooms. Note one restroom stop roughly every hour. Visitor centers, state parks and cafes are the most reliable.
  3. Bring the right cards. A disability placard opens up closer parking. See how to get a placard in New Jersey. New Jersey residents 62 and older can get a free State Park Senior Citizen Pass, and the federal Senior Pass covers Forsythe. Our guide to free and discounted things to do explains both.
  4. Set up the passenger seat. A seat cushion, a small pillow for the neck, sunglasses, water and binoculars within reach. A swivel seat cushion can make getting in and out easier.
  5. Time the medications and meals. Plan around pills and naps. A late morning start with lunch out often works best.
  6. Bring something to share. Old music from their younger years, a printed map or a list of the stops.
  7. Charge your phone. Cell service can be thin in the Pine Barrens and along Old Mine Road. Tell someone your route.

If your parent has stopped driving, a weekly drive can be one of the things they look forward to most. Our guide to when a parent stops driving has more ways to stay connected. If you would rather someone else do the driving, many senior centers run group outings. See senior bus trips in New Jersey.

faq.q: What is the best scenic drive in NJ for someone who can't walk?
faq.a: The 8-mile Wildlife Drive at the Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge near Atlantic City is made for viewing from the car. It costs $4 per car, honors the federal Senior Pass, and has accessible restrooms at headquarters.

faq.q: Where can I take my mom for a drive with a nice view near North Jersey?
faq.a: Try the Palisades Interstate Parkway northbound and stop at State Line Lookout in Alpine, which has restrooms, metered parking and an accessible cafe. High Point State Park in Wantage has views of three states and free entrance from Labor Day to Memorial Day weekend.

faq.q: How do I plan a scenic drive for my dad, who uses a walker?
faq.a: Pick a 30 to 60 minute stretch, plan a restroom stop about every hour at a visitor center or state park, and bring his disability placard and park passes. Call ahead to ask where the closest accessible parking is.

faq.q: Do I need to pay to drive the Forsythe Wildlife Drive?
faq.a: Yes, $4 per car, unless you have an America the Beautiful pass such as the Senior Pass. Passes bought at the visitor center are cash or check only. Entrance is also free on the refuge system's fee-free days, which include Veterans Day.

faq.q: What are New Jersey's scenic byways?
faq.a: NJDOT lists eight: Bayshore Heritage, Delaware River, Millstone Valley, Palisades, Pine Barrens, Upper Freehold, Warren Heritage and Western Highlands. Each is signed with its own logo, and maps are on the NJ Scenic Byways website.

faq.q: Is Old Mine Road open?
faq.a: Sections have closed for repaving and bridge work, and nearby Route 615 has been closed by a landslide. Check the Delaware Water Gap current conditions page or call 570-426-2452 before you go.
